input: In this staffing review, we take a closer look at the current resourcing arrangements for the maintenance crew and explore whether there might be scope to adjust the balance between overtime working and established staffing levels. The maintenance crew currently consists of 15 full-time members of staff, and during last year overtime accounted for 9% of paid hours, which is by no means an insignificant share of the total hours worked. It is important to note, however, that this overtime is not distributed evenly across the year; instead, it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, when the demand for maintenance work is at its highest. One potential option that has been identified is replacing half of the overtime with one additional hire, and it has been estimated that this would cost $74k per year on a fully loaded basis. That said, it is equally important to bear in mind that a hire is paid for the full year, so the additional capacity would be in place throughout the year, including during quieter periods when the overtime requirement is much lower. This creates an interesting dynamic, because overtime is inherently flexible and can be dialled up or down as circumstances require, whereas the cost of an additional hire is essentially fixed once the appointment is made. Ultimately, decision-makers will want to weigh a range of factors, including the $74k per year fully loaded cost of the hire, the 9% of paid hours currently worked as overtime by the 15 full-time staff, and the fact that this overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, before coming to a view on the best way forward for the maintenance crew.
target: The maintenance crew review turns on a mismatch of timing, and the figures state it plainly. The crew has 15 full-time staff. Overtime stood at 9% of paid hours last year. Replacing half of the overtime with one additional hire costs $74k per year fully loaded. The overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks. A hire is paid for the full year. Set side by side, the two options buy different things: overtime buys hours inside the two seasonal peaks, where the demand stands, and the hire buys hours spread across the full year, including the long stretches between the peaks when no overtime is worked. The cost of the hire, $74k per year fully loaded, is therefore not compared against the overtime it replaces alone; it is compared against peak cover bought at a year-round price. Half of the overtime would remain in place under the proposal, so the peaks would still carry an overtime element, and the crew would carry the additional hire through every non-peak week as well. The proposal also changes the form of the cost before it changes the amount of cover: a cost that now rises and falls with demand becomes a cost that runs at one level in every week of the year, peak and non-peak alike. The figures support a narrow conclusion. Where the need is peak cover only, the hire is the more expensive way to buy it, because its cost runs for the full year while the need runs for two seasonal peaks. Where cover is short outside the peaks, the case changes, but nothing in last year's figures (15 full-time staff, overtime at 9% of paid hours) speaks to a shortfall outside the peaks. A decision to hire should therefore rest on evidence about non-peak cover, which this review does not contain.
